note.explanation: A body's equilibrium state depends on what happens when it is tilted or disturbed. A stable body returns to its starting position; an unstable body moves farther away; a neutral body rests in its new position. The centre of mass and the base of support help explain whether a body topples.
examples: A cone standing on its circular base is stable: a slight tilt raises its centre of gravity, and the resulting torque brings it back.
A cylinder rolling on a flat surface is neutral: its centre of mass stays at the same height as it moves.
note.checkAnswer: A cone on its circular base is in stable equilibrium.
note.simple: Ask what the body does after a small push: return means stable, move farther away means unstable, and stay in its new position means neutral.

written.text: Discuss the concepts of stability and centre of gravity in relation to objects toppling over. Provide an example where an object’s centre of gravity affects its stability, and explain how altering its base of support can influence stability.
written.finalAnswer: An object is more stable when its centre of gravity is low and its base of support is wide. It topples if the line of action of its weight falls outside its base. For example, a cone on its base returns after a slight tilt while its centre of gravity remains above the base. Widening the base makes toppling less likely.

written.text: How the stability of an object can be improved? Give a few examples to support your answer.
written.finalAnswer: The stability of an object can be improved by lowering its centre of gravity and widening its base of support. For example, racing cars are made low and broad, and balancing toys are designed with their weight low down.

example.question: A cone stands on its circular base and is tilted slightly. Identify its state of equilibrium and explain what happens.
example.answer: The cone is in stable equilibrium; it returns to its original position.

explain.title: Equilibrium and support
explain.body: An object is balanced when its centre of mass and its point of support lie on the same vertical line. Then forces on each side are balanced, and the object is said to be in equilibrium.

explain.title: Stable equilibrium
explain.body: A body is said to be in a state of stable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it comes back to its original position. A cone on its circular base is stable: tilting raises its centre of gravity, and the resulting torque brings it back.

explain.title: Unstable equilibrium
explain.body: A body is said to be in a state of unstable equilibrium, if after a slight tilt, it tends to move on further away from its original position. A cone balanced on its tip is unstable because tilting makes it fall farther away.

explain.title: Neutral equilibrium
explain.body: A body is in neutral equilibrium, if it comes to rest in its new position after disturbance without any change in its centre of mass. A cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface is an example because the height of its centre of mass remains unchanged.

explain.title: The base of support and toppling
explain.body: A body remains in equilibrium as long as its centre of mass lies within the base. If the line of action of its weight no longer lies inside the base, the body can topple.

mistakes: Do not mix up stable and unstable: stable returns after a slight tilt; unstable moves farther away.
Do not call every object that moves unstable. A rolling cylinder can show neutral equilibrium if its centre of mass stays at the same height.
Do not say a body topples simply because it is tilted; explain whether the line of action of its weight lies outside its base.
Do not confuse the centre of mass with the base of support; both are needed when explaining toppling.
